name: Mendel and the 28,000 pea plants
scope: The monk who counted, and the 34 years nobody read him. T1: in the garden of St Thomas's Abbey in Brno, an Augustinian friar spent eight years (1856-1863) opening pea flowers with tweezers to strip out the anthers, brushing pollen on by hand and bagging the blossoms so no bee could interfere -- roughly 28,000 plants, one trait at a time (the hook: the first law of heredity came out of a monastery vegetable patch). T2: what the counting showed -- cross two true-breeding peas and the offspring all look like ONE parent, but let those self-pollinate and the vanished form comes BACK, at a stubborn ratio near 3:1 (5,474 round seeds to 1,850 wrinkled; 6,022 yellow to 2,001 green; 787 tall to 277 short). T3: why that killed the reigning idea -- 'blending' inheritance held that parents' traits mixed like paints, so a recessive form should be diluted away forever; peas proved heredity travels as particles that can hide for a whole generation and reappear undiluted. T4: the two-trait run -- 315 round-yellow : 101 round-green : 108 wrinkled-yellow : 32 wrinkled-green, the 9:3:3:1 showing seed shape and seed colour are dealt out independently of each other. T4: Mendel had to fight the pea's own biology -- peas self-pollinate, which is exactly why they breed true, and exactly why every single cross had to be done by hand. T5: his own follow-up FAILED -- the eminent botanist Carl Naegeli told him to repeat the work in hawkweed (Hieracium), and 5,000-plus crosses from 1869-1873 produced no clean ratios, because many hawkweeds set seed asexually (apomixis) and never shuffle anything: the right law, tested in the wrong organism. T5: the burial -- the 1866 paper 'Versuche ueber Pflanzen-Hybriden' drew only a handful of citations in 34 years, and his election as abbot on 30 March 1868 buried him in estate accounts and tax disputes; he died in 1884 with the laws still unread. T5: the resurrection -- in 1900 Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak independently hit the same ratios in three different plants and each went back and cited the forgotten Brno paper. T5: the uncomfortable audit -- in 1936 R. A. Fisher ran chi-square tests on Mendel's tables and found the counts fit theory TOO closely (joint odds on the order of 1 in 20,000 or worse); Fisher suspected unconscious bias or an assistant's helpful sorting rather than fraud, modern replications confirm the laws, and the episode is the bank's model of science auditing even its saints.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (primary; 28,000 plants 1856-1863, seven traits, 5,474:1,850 and 6,022:2,001 and 787:277 counts, 315:101:108:32 dihybrid, Feb 8 / Mar 8 1865 lectures, 1866 Verhandlungen paper, Naegeli correspondence from 31 Dec 1866, 5,000+ Hieracium crosses 1869-1873 and apomixis, abbot 30 Mar 1868, death 1884, Fisher 1936 chi-square analysis and the fraud debate, 1900 rediscovery by de Vries/Correns/Tschermak); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregor_Mendel
framing_note: The flagship DISCOVERY-plus-neglect ladder and the sub-strand's best 'the test decides, not the audience' story. T1 keys the ACT (hand-pollinating and counting 28,000 plants), never a date and never the word genetics -- Mendel never used it. Accuracy rails: Mendel wrote of 'factors', NOT genes (Johannsen coined 'gene' in 1909) and he did not discover DNA or chromosomes; his ratios are approximations from large counts (2.96:1, 3.01:1, 2.84:1) so never present 3:1 as an exact result; the Fisher rung says 'fits theory too well, probably unconscious bias', NEVER 'Mendel faked it', and must end with the laws standing. Dinner-test payoff: the hawkweed rung -- the man who found the law of heredity spent four years failing to reproduce it because he picked a plant that skips sex. Distractor mine: blending inheritance, Darwin's own pangenesis/gemmules (which Mendel's letters to Naegeli quietly contradicted), Lamarckian use-inheritance, and the three real rediscoverers used as choices for one another. Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'traits are carried as discrete particles' before asking what the 3:1 ratio overturned -- describe the vanished wrinkled peas coming back and let the doctrine be recalled.
history_overlap: history bank likely owns Lysenko's suppression of Mendelian genetics as a Soviet political episode (and the science bank's own dissent/censorship strand owns Vavilov) -- this ladder must stay in the pea garden, the hawkweed failure and the 34-year neglect, and must never become a Soviet-politics rung.

name: The molecule nobody believed in: nuclein to Chargaff's ratios
scope: Why every serious scientist bet on protein, and what broke the bet. T2: in the winter of 1869, in Felix Hoppe-Seyler's laboratory -- literally a converted kitchen in Tuebingen Castle -- a young Swiss physician collected pus-soaked surgical bandages from the town hospital, washed the white blood cells off them, digested away the proteins with pepsin and precipitated a strange substance out of the cell nuclei: Friedrich Miescher's 'nuclein' (the hook: the stuff of genes was first scooped off used surgical dressings). T3: what made nuclein obviously NOT a protein -- roughly 2.5% phosphorus, no sulfur at all, and it shrugged off pepsin, the enzyme that destroys proteins. T3: Hoppe-Seyler refused to let it out for two years and made his own students repeat the entire extraction first; the paper appeared in 1871 -- replication before publication, a supervisor's skepticism doing exactly the job skepticism is for. T4: the wrong idea that made DNA look stupid -- Phoebus Levene's 'tetranucleotide hypothesis' held that DNA was a monotonous repeat of the four bases in equal amounts, a molecule far too simple to spell out an organism; proteins, with twenty different amino acids, looked like the only alphabet rich enough to write a creature. T5: the numbers that broke it -- after reading Avery's 1944 result, Erwin Chargaff turned his whole Columbia laboratory over to measuring DNA bases by acid hydrolysis and paper chromatography, and by 1950 published the rule that within any species adenine equals thymine and guanine equals cytosine, while the overall base composition varies enormously BETWEEN species. Monotony was dead, and the pairing clue was sitting in a table of numbers three years before anyone drew a helix. T5: Chargaff measured the ratios but never saw the ladder in them -- he met Watson and Crick in Cambridge in 1952, told them what his lab had found, and thought little of them; he spent the rest of his life resenting what they built out of his numbers. T5: Miescher himself, in private letters as early as 1892, wondered whether nuclein might carry heredity -- and never made the argument in public.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Miescher (1869 Tuebingen, Hoppe-Seyler's castle-kitchen lab, pus-soaked bandages, pepsin digestion, ~2.5% phosphorus and no sulfur, 1871 publication after student verification, 1892 letters); grokipedia.com/page/Erwin_Chargaff (1944 pivot prompted by Avery, hydrolysis + paper chromatography, A=T G=C published 1950, rejection of Levene's tetranucleotide hypothesis, May 1952 Cambridge meeting with Watson and Crick, Heraclitean Fire 1978)
framing_note: The 'why the wrong consensus was reasonable' ladder -- it is the distractor mine for this entire sub-strand, built as a topic in its own right. Voice: steelman the protein bet fully before dismantling it; the kid should finish able to explain WHY clever people were wrong, not merely that they were. Dinner-test payoff: the pus-bandages rung. Accuracy rails: Miescher isolated 'nuclein' (a nuclear extract including what we now call DNA), he did NOT isolate pure DNA and did NOT show it carried heredity; Levene's tetranucleotide idea was a defensible reading of genuinely poor analytical data, not idiocy -- present it as the best available inference of its day. Any Chargaff quotation must come from a documented source (Heraclitean Fire, 1978) or be paraphrased rather than invented. Distractor mine: protein-as-the-gene, the tetranucleotide hypothesis, 'nuclein is the cell's phosphorus store', Kossel's base chemistry. Anti-restatement: never state that nuclein contains no sulfur in the same stem that asks what distinguished it from protein.

name: Proving the gene is DNA: Griffith, Avery, Hershey and Chase
scope: Three experiments, one question: what carries heredity? T1: in 1928 Frederick Griffith injected mice four ways -- live harmless rough pneumococci alone (mice fine), heat-killed deadly smooth pneumococci alone (mice fine), live deadly smooth (mice die), and the combination of LIVE harmless plus HEAT-KILLED deadly. That last group died, and living, fully deadly capsuled bacteria were recovered from their blood: something in the dead cells had permanently taught the living ones. T2: Griffith was not hunting genes at all -- he was a Ministry of Health medical officer trying to build a better pneumonia vaccine and asking whether pneumococcal types were stable, which is why he was mixing types in the first place. T2: the change bred true -- the transformed bacteria stayed deadly through generation after generation in culture, so whatever moved was heritable, not a temporary infection. T3: Griffith never found out what it was; he was killed in a London air raid in 1941, three years before the answer. T3: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty spent more than a decade at the Rockefeller Institute purifying Griffith's 'transforming principle' out of 50-75 litre broth batches of heat-killed Type III pneumococci. T4: the elimination logic -- destroy each candidate in turn and see which destruction stops the effect. Trypsin and chymotrypsin (protein-destroyers): transforming power survived. Ribonuclease (RNA): survived. Deoxyribonuclease: the power vanished completely. Published 1944 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. T4: before he published, Avery wrote his brother Roy a long 1943 letter working through what he had -- and the line 'Sounds like a virus -- may be a gene' (a careful man's private excitement, kept out of print). T5: the reception -- Alfred Mirsky argued the preparations were contaminated with a trace of protein and held that position into the early 1950s; Avery never received a Nobel Prize (the Royal Society gave him its Copley Medal in 1945). Erwin Chargaff, by contrast, called the work epochal and redirected his entire laboratory because of it. T4: Hershey and Chase's trick in 1952 -- DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur; protein contains sulfur but no phosphorus. So grow T2 bacteriophage with radioactive phosphorus-32 to tag its DNA and radioactive sulfur-35 to tag its protein coat, and let the tagged phages infect ordinary E. coli. T5: the kitchen appliance -- to strip the spent phage coats off the bacterial surface they ran the culture in a Waring blender, then spun it in a centrifuge: the phosphorus-32 rode down in the bacterial pellet, the sulfur-35 stayed up in the liquid. The DNA went in; the protein stayed outside. T5: the honest caveat -- some sulfur did get in and some phosphorus stayed out, and Hershey and Chase wrote cautiously, claiming only that DNA had 'some function' rather than declaring it the gene; the community was convinced as much by the double helix arriving a year later as by the blender. T5: what Griffith actually stumbled into has a modern name -- horizontal gene transfer, the same trick by which bacteria hand each other antibiotic resistance today.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Griffith%27s_experiment (1928 four-group mouse design, R/S strains, heat-killing at 60C, heritable stable transformation, vaccine motive, Griffith killed in a 1941 London air raid, Dawson & Sia 1931 in vitro replication, Alloway 1932 cell-free extracts); grokipedia.com/page/Avery-MacLeod-McCarty_experiment (50-75 litre batches, trypsin/chymotrypsin/RNase/DNase elimination, 1944 J Exp Med, Mirsky's contamination objection into the early 1950s, no Nobel, Copley Medal 1945, Chargaff calling it epochal); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hershey-Chase_experiment (1952, T2 phage, 32P/35S rationale, blender + centrifuge, Hershey and Chase's own cautious conclusion); profiles.nlm.nih.gov Oswald T. Avery Profiles in Science (1943 letter to Roy Avery, 'Sounds like a virus -- may be a gene')
framing_note: A CONCEPT/THEME ladder with the analytic backbone this sub-strand needs: the spine is one question (what is the hereditary material?) and every rung is a named case answering it. Dinner-test payoff: the kitchen blender rung -- the question of what genes are made of was settled with an appliance you can buy. Accuracy rails: (1) Griffith showed only that SOMETHING transferable and heritable existed -- he said nothing about DNA, and a rung must never credit him with it; (2) the Hershey-Chase result was suggestive rather than airtight and the authors said so -- the corrected-misconception version ('the blender proved it once and for all') is the one to teach against; (3) Avery's team is three names, use all three. Any use of the Avery letter must quote the documented phrase and date it to 1943. Distractor mine is exceptionally rich here and entirely real: protein as the hereditary material (the live consensus of serious people), the polysaccharide capsule, RNA, 'a virus', and protein contamination of the DNA prep -- Mirsky's objection was a legitimate scientific criticism, not stubbornness, and should be framed that way. Anti-restatement: describe what the mice DID (which group died, what was recovered from their blood) and let the meaning be recalled knowledge; never say 'DNA carries heredity' in a stem asking what the DNase treatment showed.
history_overlap: history bank owns the London Blitz as a WWII episode -- the Griffith rung must key his unfinished discovery (he died without ever learning what his transforming principle was), never the air war itself.

name: Photo 51 and the honest credit story
scope: The best photograph anyone had ever taken of DNA, and what happened to the woman who took it. T1: on 6 May 1952, in a basement laboratory at King's College London, Rosalind Franklin and her PhD student Raymond Gosling aimed X-rays at a hair-thin bundle of hydrated DNA fibres and left the film exposed for 62 hours. The fifty-first photograph in the series came out with a stark black X across the middle. T2: what the X means -- an X-shaped diffraction pattern is the signature of a helix, and nothing else makes it. T3: the numbers hidden in the spacings -- a repeat of about 34 angstroms with a strong reflection at 3.4 angstroms, meaning roughly ten steps per full turn; the pattern also placed the phosphate backbone on the OUTSIDE of the molecule. T3: why her image beat everyone's -- Franklin built a humidity chamber and held the fibres at about 75% relative humidity to lock DNA into its wet 'B' form, the form that exists inside living cells; earlier pictures by Astbury and by Wilkins had mixed the dry A form with the wet B form and blurred both. T4: the moment -- on 30 January 1953 Maurice Wilkins showed the photograph to James Watson without Franklin's knowledge or consent; separately, a Medical Research Council progress report containing her measurements reached Francis Crick through Max Perutz. T4: Franklin was neither anti-helix nor adrift -- her own manuscript went in before Watson and Crick's model was published and appeared in the SAME 25 April 1953 issue of Nature, the third of three papers; her method was to derive the structure from data rather than to build models first, which was slower and, on her own terms, more rigorous. T5: the arithmetic of the Nobel, told straight -- Franklin died of ovarian cancer on 16 April 1958, aged 37; the prize went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins in 1962. A Nobel is not awarded posthumously and no more than three people may share one: she was not passed over by the committee, because she had been dead four years. T5: so what WAS the wrong done to her? Her data were shown to a competitor without her consent, the 1953 papers thanked King's for 'unpublished results' without saying what those results had settled, and Watson's 1968 memoir 'The Double Helix' caricatured her as 'Rosy' -- a portrait Watson himself later conceded in an epilogue to his own book was unjust. T5: her second act -- from March 1953 at Birkbeck she produced the finest X-ray work then existing on tobacco mosaic virus, locating its RNA inside the protein helix, and had begun on poliovirus when she died; her collaborator Aaron Klug won the 1982 Nobel for work that grew directly out of hers.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Photo_51 (6 May 1952, Franklin and Gosling, 62-hour exposure, 34 A pitch and 3.4 A rise, backbone outside, humidity control at ~75% RH, Wilkins showing it to Watson on 30 January 1953 without consent, MRC report via Perutz, the three 25 April 1953 Nature papers, defenders' and critics' cases both stated); grokipedia.com/page/Rosalind_Franklin (born 25 July 1920, died 16 April 1958 aged 37 of ovarian cancer, Birkbeck TMV work from March 1953, RNA at 42 A radius, poliovirus project 1957-58, Klug's 1982 Nobel); nobelprize.org (1962 Physiology or Medicine to Watson, Crick, Wilkins)
framing_note: vision_mandated TRUE: this is the sub-strand's credit-and-institutions rung and BOTH failure modes are live -- a hagiographic 'stolen Nobel' morality play (factually wrong) and a dismissive 'she was only a technician' (also wrong). The bank PRESENTS the documented record and lets the kid weigh it; no sermon in either direction, no DEI reframing, no erasure. Accuracy rails, non-negotiable: (1) Photo 51 was produced by Franklin AND Gosling, with Gosling operating the camera -- name both; (2) Franklin was NOT denied the prize by the Nobel committee, she was dead four years before it was given and Nobels are not awarded posthumously -- a rung that says otherwise is a factual error the bank must instead CORRECT, which makes this a corrected-misconception rung and therefore on-voice gold; (3) the genuine grievances are the unconsented sharing of her data and Watson's memoir, and Watson's own later retraction is part of the record. Dinner-test payoff: the 62-hour exposure rung -- one photograph, two and a half days of X-rays. Distractor mine: real adjacent people used as choices (Wilkins, Gosling, Astbury, Perutz, Klug, Pauling) and real rival readings of the diffraction pattern. Anti-restatement: never say 'the X-shape indicates a helix' in a stem that asks what the X-shape showed.

name: The double helix and the sentence at the end
scope: A structure that gives away its own function. T1: the model that changed biology was built out of cut metal plates and clamps in a Cambridge workshop -- Watson and Crick ran no experiment of their own on DNA, and their one-page Nature paper of 25 April 1953 contains no data at all. T2: the fit that made it click -- Chargaff's finding that adenine always equals thymine and guanine always equals cytosine only makes sense if A sits opposite T and G opposite C; a large purine paired with a small pyrimidine keeps the ladder exactly the same width all the way down, no matter what sequence is written on it. T2: A-T is held by two hydrogen bonds and G-C by three, which is why DNA rich in G and C needs more heat to pull apart -- a prediction of the model that any lab can test. T3: the secret built into the shape -- because each strand carries the complete instructions for making the other, the structure ITSELF answers how a cell copies its genes. The paper's closing line, one of the most famous sentences in science: 'It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.' T3: the two strands run in OPPOSITE directions and the sugar-phosphate backbone is on the outside, leaving the bases stacked inside like the treads of a spiral staircase. T4: it is the stacking of those flat bases, not the hydrogen bonds between them, that supplies most of the molecule's stability -- the usual textbook picture gets the strongest force wrong. T4: the greatest chemist alive got it wrong FIRST -- in February 1953 Linus Pauling published a THREE-stranded model with the phosphates crammed into the core and, worse, un-ionized: a structure in which deoxyribonucleic ACID is not an acid, and in which the negative phosphates at the axis would tear the molecule apart. Watson and Crick saw the error at once. T4: Watson's own first guess was wrong too -- he tried pairing like with like (A with A, G with G), which cannot give a constant width; the chemist Jerry Donohue told him he was using the wrong tautomeric forms of the bases, and correcting that produced A-T and G-C the same afternoon. T5: what the structure did NOT explain -- nothing about how a sequence of bases becomes a protein. That took another eight years and a different set of people. T5: the packing problem it created -- about two metres of DNA in every human cell nucleus a few thousandths of a millimetre across, solved by winding roughly 147 base pairs around each of millions of protein spools.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Nucleic_acid_double_helix (April 1953 model, antiparallel strands, A-T two H-bonds and G-C three, 3.4 nm pitch and ~10 bp per turn, base stacking supplying ~70% of duplex stability, ~147 bp per histone octamer from Klug's nucleosome work, Chargaff's rules as constraint); Watson & Crick, 'Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids', Nature 171, 25 April 1953 (closing sentence, verbatim); paulingblog.wordpress.com and retractionwatch.com coverage of the Pauling-Corey February 1953 PNAS triple-helix model and its un-ionized central phosphates
framing_note: The MECHANISM flagship of the sub-strand: the answer to every rung is a specific structural fact or a specific consequence of it, never the bare phrase 'the double helix'. Dinner-test payoff: Pauling's triple helix -- the most decorated chemist of the century published a DNA model in which the acid was not acidic. Accuracy rails: the closing sentence is the bank's one documented quotation here and must be reproduced EXACTLY and attributed to the 25 April 1953 Nature paper; the bank states plainly that Watson and Crick built a MODEL out of other people's measurements (Franklin's dimensions, Chargaff's ratios, Donohue's tautomer correction) -- that is not a slur, it is how theoretical work is done, and saying it protects the kid from the lone-genius myth; base stacking, not hydrogen bonding, dominates stability -- teach the term 'hydrogen bond' before testing it. Distractor mine: Pauling's triple helix, like-with-like pairing (Watson's own first wrong guess), a bases-outside/backbone-inside model, and the wrong enol tautomers Donohue corrected -- every one a real wrong idea held by a real expert. Lane border: Franklin's credit story is a separate ladder; keep this one on the STRUCTURE and its consequences.

name: Meselson and Stahl: the most beautiful experiment
scope: How to design an experiment that three theories cannot survive together. T3: after 1953 there were three live accounts of how DNA copies itself -- conservative (the original double helix stays intact and an entirely new one is built beside it), semiconservative (the strands part and each templates a new partner, so every daughter molecule is half old), and dispersive (Max Delbrueck's 1954 proposal: the old DNA is chopped and interleaved with new stretches along both strands). All three explain the same fact, so an argument could not settle it. T3: the trick -- Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl grew E. coli for about fourteen generations on the heavy stable isotope nitrogen-15 until every nitrogen atom in its DNA was heavy, then transferred the bacteria into ordinary nitrogen-14 and tracked WEIGHT, not radioactivity. T4: the readout -- spin the extracted DNA for about twenty hours in a caesium chloride solution until the salt itself settles into a density gradient, and each DNA molecule floats to the exact depth matching its own density; photograph the bands by ultraviolet absorption. T4: the killer result at generation one -- a SINGLE band, at precisely intermediate density, with no heavy band anywhere. Conservative replication requires the original heavy molecule to persist forever; one photograph destroyed it. T5: generation two gave TWO bands, intermediate and light, in equal amounts. Dispersive replication predicts one band drifting steadily lighter and never splitting in two; that killed it. Only semiconservative replication predicted both pictures, and it was right. T5: the precision was extraordinary -- densities of 1.724, 1.717 and 1.710 grams per cubic centimetre resolved to about a thousandth, and the sharpness of the bands also proved the DNA had not been broken during extraction. T5: John Cairns called it 'the most beautiful experiment in biology' (recorded in Horace Judson's 'The Eighth Day of Creation'), and the beauty is entirely in the design: three theories were made to predict three DIFFERENT photographs before the film was developed.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Meselson-Stahl_experiment (1957-58 at Caltech under Norman Davidson, ~14 generations on 15NH4Cl at 96.5% isotopic purity, transfer to 14N, CsCl equilibrium density gradient at 44,770 rpm for ~20 hours, band densities 1.724 / 1.717 / 1.710 g/cm3, generation-1 single hybrid band, generation-2 equal hybrid and light bands, Delbrueck's 1954 dispersive model); whyevolutionistrue.com and ibiology.org on the John Cairns attribution via Judson's 'The Eighth Day of Creation'
framing_note: The sub-strand's model of experimental DESIGN -- a CONCEPT ladder whose wonder is the shape of the test, not the answer. Dinner-test payoff: the single intermediate band at generation one, which erased one whole theory in a single photograph. Accuracy rail (the big one): nitrogen-15 is a STABLE heavy isotope, NOT radioactive -- this experiment measures weight, and confusing it with Hershey-Chase's radioactive labels is the standard classroom error, so the bank should teach 'isotope' explicitly before testing it and may build a corrected-misconception rung on exactly this. Second rail: the conservative and dispersive models were REAL positions held by real scientists (Delbrueck for dispersive), so they are honest distractors, not straw men. Distractor mine: the two rival replication models, radioactive labelling, electron microscopy, and Watson-Crick's prediction attributed to the wrong people. Anti-restatement: a stem may describe the observed bands OR name the three models, never both -- if it does both, the kid deduces instead of knowing.

name: Cracking the code: Nirenberg's poly-U
scope: Reading the first word of the genetic language. T2: the puzzle stated in numbers -- four bases must somehow specify twenty amino acids. George Gamow reasoned in 1954 that pairs of bases give only sixteen combinations, too few, while triplets give sixty-four, more than enough; his specific proposal, an overlapping 'diamond code', was wrong in every detail except the number three. T3: proving the code is read in NON-overlapping threes -- in 1961 Crick, Brenner and colleagues used acridine chemicals to insert or delete single bases in a phage gene: one insertion wrecked the protein, two wrecked it, but THREE insertions restored a working protein, because the reading frame had snapped back into register. T2: the moment -- at about three o'clock in the morning on 27 May 1961, in a laboratory at the NIH, Heinrich Matthaei added a synthetic RNA made of nothing but uracil (poly-U) to a cell-free extract of E. coli, with each of the twenty amino acids radiolabelled in a separate tube. Only the phenylalanine tube built protein. UUU means phenylalanine -- the first word of the genetic language ever read, and read out of an RNA that no organism had ever made. T4: the Moscow scene -- in August 1961 the unknown Nirenberg presented the result at the International Congress of Biochemistry to an audience of about thirty-five people; word reached Francis Crick, who arranged for him to give the talk again to roughly a thousand, and he was applauded off the stage. T4: how the other sixty-three words fell -- Nirenberg and Philip Leder's 1964 trinucleotide-binding assay, in which a filter traps a ribosome only when the transfer RNA matches the three-letter code word, plus Har Gobind Khorana's synthetic repeating polymers as independent confirmation; by 1965 fifty-four of the sixty-four triplets were assigned. The 1968 Nobel went to Nirenberg, Khorana and Holley. T5: the shape of the finished table -- sixty-four code words for twenty amino acids means built-in redundancy, concentrated in the third letter, so a great many single-letter typos change nothing at all; and three triplets, UAA, UAG and UGA, spell no amino acid and mean STOP. T5: the same table runs in bacteria, oak trees, whales and humans, with small deviations in mitochondria and a few microbes -- near-universality is among the strongest evidence that everything alive descends from a common ancestor. T5: Nirenberg was a salaried government scientist at the NIH, the first federal employee to take the Nobel in Physiology or Medicine, working against the most famous laboratories in the field.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Marshall_Warren_Nirenberg (Matthaei's poly-U tube at ~3:00 a.m. on 27 May 1961, cell-free E. coli extract, C-14 labelled amino acids in separate tubes, Moscow August 1961 congress, Leder trinucleotide-binding assay 1964, 54 of 64 triplets by 1965, AUG initiation, Nobel 17 October 1968 with Khorana and Holley, first federal employee to win it); grokipedia.com/page/Genetic_code (degeneracy, wobble, non-overlapping comma-less reading, frameshift consequences, near-universality with mitochondrial exceptions); grokipedia.com/page/George_Gamow (1954 triplet reasoning, 4^3=64); sciencehistory.org 'Breaking the Code' and lindahall.org (the ~35-person first talk and Crick arranging the repeat before ~1,000)
framing_note: Dinner-test payoff: the three-in-the-morning poly-U tube -- a made-up RNA that says nothing but 'UUU UUU UUU' and a soup of broken-open bacteria that answers with one amino acid. Accuracy rails: Matthaei ran the decisive tube, so name him and not only Nirenberg; Gamow's diamond code was WRONG in its mechanism but his counting argument (4 cubed is 64) was right, and the bank tells it that way rather than as a simple blunder; the code is NEARLY universal, never 'universal' -- mitochondria and some ciliates read it differently, and that caveat is itself a good rung. Distractor mine: Gamow's overlapping diamond code, a two-letter code, a code with 'commas' between words, and the real rivals Khorana, Holley and Ochoa used as named alternatives to Nirenberg. Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'the code is read in non-overlapping triplets' before asking what the frameshift experiment established -- describe what happened when one, two and three bases were added, and let the conclusion be recalled. Lane border: 'what a good test looks like' belongs to science as WORKING PRACTICE; keep Popper and the philosophy seminar out of it.

name: McClintock's jumping genes
scope: The genes that move, and the martyr story that turns out to be half a myth. T2: the readout was a corn cob you could hold in your hand -- kernels streaked, spotted and sectored with colour where there should have been none. T3: what Barbara McClintock traced the speckles to -- a piece of chromosome she called Dissociation (Ds) lands inside the colour gene and switches it off, and a second element, Activator (Ac), can pop it back out partway through the kernel's development; every cell descended from that one cell then makes pigment, and the patch of colour on the kernel is that family of cells made visible. Published in PNAS in 1950. T3: why this was heresy -- the whole triumph of genetics up to that point was mapping genes as beads fixed in a fixed order along a string. McClintock was saying some of the beads get up and move. T4: the 1951 Cold Spring Harbor Symposium -- she presented the evidence to an audience that included George Beadle and Salvador Luria and met puzzlement rather than argument; by the mid-1950s she had stopped giving talks on controlling elements and largely stopped publishing on them, her last major paper on the subject appearing in 1956. T4: vindication arrived from bacteria, not corn -- insertion sequences found moving in E. coli from 1968, then transposons cloned and sequenced through the 1970s; the 1983 Nobel in Physiology or Medicine went to McClintock ALONE, and she remains the only woman to hold an unshared prize in that category. T5 (corrected misconception): the popular story of a woman ignored for thirty years is itself partly a myth. She was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1944, only its third woman, and was made the first woman president of the Genetics Society of America in 1945; the historian Nathaniel Comfort's archival work ('The Tangled Field', 2001) shows she remained a distinguished figure throughout the decades of her supposed rejection. What her colleagues resisted was her CLAIM, not her standing -- which is a more useful lesson than martyrdom. T5: the scale of what she found -- transposable elements and their broken remains make up roughly half of the human genome and 40-80% of many plant genomes. T5 (still open): are they machinery or parasites? Orgel and Crick, and Doolittle and Sapienza, argued in 1980 that most transposons are 'selfish DNA' propagating at the host's expense; McClintock argued they were controllers. The honest modern answer is that both happen, and telling which is which in any particular case is unfinished work.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Barbara_McClintock (maize aleurone variegation, Ac/Ds mechanism, 1950 PNAS 'The Origin and Behavior of Mutable Loci in Maize', 1951 Cold Spring Harbor Symposium 4-8 June and its reception, ceased presenting by mid-decade with last major paper 1956, E. coli insertion sequences 1968 Saedler and Starlinger, Ac cloned 1984 by Fedoroff, National Medal of Science 1970, Wolf and Lasker Prizes 1981, unshared 1983 Nobel, selfish-DNA debate, transposons at 40-80% of plant and animal genomes); Nathaniel Comfort, 'The Tangled Field' (Harvard UP, 2001) via hup.harvard.edu; NLM Profiles in Science and Britannica for NAS election 1944 (third woman) and Genetics Society of America presidency 1945 (first woman)
framing_note: A REVERSAL ladder whose T5 is a corrected-misconception rung -- exactly the bank's voice: the martyr story is half true, and the true half is more interesting than the legend. Accuracy rails: she was NOT shunned, unfunded or unemployed -- NAS 1944, GSA president 1945, a permanent Carnegie post at Cold Spring Harbor, National Medal of Science 1970; what stalled was acceptance of transposition, not her career, and the bank must say that plainly rather than repeat the neglected-genius script. Her own term was 'controlling elements'; 'transposon' came later. 'Selfish DNA' is Orgel & Crick and Doolittle & Sapienza, both 1980 -- date it correctly. Dinner-test payoff: the speckled kernel -- a genetics experiment you can pick up off a farm-stand table, which makes this ladder's T1/T2 a genuine test-it-yourself invitation (buy Indian corn, look at the sectors, ask what each patch is a family of). Distractor mine: fixed bead-on-a-string gene mapping, ordinary spontaneous mutation, viral contamination, chromosome breakage alone, paramutation -- all real and all adjacent. Anti-restatement: never let a stem describe an element inserting and excising before asking what caused the speckling.
history_overlap: cooking bank owns maize and corn as an ingredient and as food history -- this ladder must key the cob as a genetic READOUT (the sectors are cell lineages), never as food.

name: One letter: sickle cell from Herrick's slide to the malaria bargain
scope: Following a whole disease down to a single letter, and then finding out why the letter survives. T3: in 1910 the Chicago physician James Herrick examined blood from a twenty-year-old dental student from Grenada suffering severe anaemia, breathlessness and leg ulcers, and found red cells drawn out into long curved sickle shapes. A disease named for a SHAPE, four decades before anyone could say why the shape appeared. T3: in 1949 Linus Pauling, with Harvey Itano, S. J. Singer and Ibert Wells, ran normal and sickle haemoglobin through an electrophoresis cell and found the two proteins drifted at different speeds -- they carried different electrical charge. Pauling's paper coined a category that did not exist before: a 'molecular disease', a whole illness traced to one wrong molecule. T4: in 1956-57, at the Cavendish Laboratory under Max Perutz, Vernon Ingram chopped haemoglobin into peptide fragments and spread them on paper -- electrophoresis in one direction, chromatography at right angles -- producing a two-dimensional 'fingerprint' of spots. Normal and sickle fingerprints were identical except for a single spot sitting in the wrong place. One peptide. Then, within that peptide, one amino acid: glutamic acid replaced by valine at position six of the beta chain. T4: in DNA terms it is a single base out of three billion -- the codon GAG becomes GTG. The swap trades a water-loving residue for a greasy one, and in low oxygen the greasy patch lets haemoglobin molecules stack into stiff fibres that warp the whole cell. T5: the puzzle J. B. S. Haldane posed in 1949 -- if two copies of this allele are often lethal in childhood, natural selection should have scrubbed it out; why is it common? T5: the answer, tested in the field in East Africa by Anthony Allison in the 1950s -- ONE copy protects against severe falciparum malaria. Where malaria was endemic the allele runs at 10-20%; where malaria never was, it is close to zero. The gene's map is the mosquito's map. T5: this is natural selection caught in the act in a living human population, with its arithmetic fully visible and fully cruel -- the same allele that saves one child kills another, and no amount of wishing changes the trade.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Sickle_cell_disease (Herrick November 1910 and the Grenadian dental student, Pauling/Itano/Singer/Wells 1949 electrophoresis and 'first molecular disease', HBB codon 6 GAG to GTG giving Glu to Val, hydrophobic patch and deoxy polymerisation, heterozygote advantage against P. falciparum, HbS allele frequencies 5-20% in sub-Saharan Africa and near zero in malaria-free regions, Mediterranean/Arabian/Indian distributions, Gabon cohort mortality data); genome.gov '1956: Cause of Disease Traced to Alteration' and thelancet.com obituary of Vernon Ingram (1956-57 Cavendish peptide fingerprinting under Perutz, 'father of molecular medicine')
framing_note: A short analytic ladder that closes the loop from DNA letter to living consequence, and the sub-strand's one place where the evolution MECHANISM shows up with a human dataset behind it. Dinner-test payoff: Ingram's fingerprint -- two sheets of paper, hundreds of identical spots, and one spot in the wrong place. Accuracy rails: Pauling's team showed a CHARGE difference between the two haemoglobins, Ingram found the amino acid -- do not merge the two into one discovery, seven years apart is the point; carriers are generally healthy but not superhuman (rare complications under extreme exertion or altitude are documented); and never present sickle cell as 'an African disease' -- it tracks the historical range of malaria, which is why it appears in Greek, Sicilian, Arabian and central Indian populations too. Distractor mine: real adjacent wrong explanations -- an infection, a vitamin deficiency, a clotting disorder, a whole missing gene rather than one substituted letter -- plus real adjacent scientists (Perutz, Itano, Haldane, Allison) as named choices. Anti-restatement: describe what Allison SAW in the field (allele frequency tracking malaria's range, carrier children surviving) and let heterozygote protection be recalled, not deduced.
history_overlap: animal bank owns the mosquito and the malaria parasite as creatures, and geography may tour malarial regions -- this ladder owns the human genetics and Allison's field EVIDENCE for carrier protection, not the insect or the place.

name: PCR: the idea on Highway 128
scope: Copying DNA a billionfold, from a hot spring and a night drive. T1: one Friday night in April 1983 Kary Mullis was driving up California Highway 128 toward his cabin in Mendocino when the scheme arrived; he pulled over near mile marker 46.7, found paper and a pen in the glove compartment, and worked it out on the roadside, then drew diagrams on every flat surface in the cabin until dawn. T2: the idea itself is almost embarrassingly simple -- heat DNA until the two strands come apart, cool it so two short synthetic primers latch on either side of the stretch you want, let a polymerase fill in the gap, then do the whole thing again. Each round doubles what you have, so thirty rounds is about a billionfold. T3: the problem that nearly killed it -- the heating step that separates the strands also destroys the polymerase, so at first a technician had to add fresh enzyme by hand at every single cycle, all day. T3: where the fix came from -- a heat-proof polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium Thomas Brock and Hudson Freeze had scooped out of a near-boiling Yellowstone hot spring in 1969 while asking whether anything at all could live at those temperatures. Taq polymerase works AT the heat that wrecks other enzymes, so the tube can simply be cycled and left alone (the wonder: curiosity-driven microbiology in a hot spring paid off fifteen years later in every crime lab on Earth). T4: what it made possible -- usable quantities of DNA from a single hair root, a smear of blood, a swab of a nose, or a five-thousand-year-old bone; the COVID test that swabs a nose is a PCR test, and so is the paternity test and the crime-scene profile. T4: the sensitivity is also the danger -- PCR will amplify a stray contaminating molecule just as faithfully as your sample, which is why serious labs run negative controls, use separate rooms for before and after amplification, and why 'detected' and 'a live infection' are not the same statement. T5: the money -- Cetus Corporation owned the patent, Mullis received a $10,000 bonus for it, and in 1991 Cetus sold the PCR patents to Hoffmann-La Roche for $300 million. Mullis shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Michael Smith. T5: the honest caveat that closes the ladder -- the same Nobel laureate spent years publicly denying that HIV causes AIDS, a claim the evidence does not support, and rejecting human-caused climate change. A Nobel Prize is awarded for a piece of work, not as a certificate that its holder is right about everything afterwards. The rule cuts both ways: an authority's credentials are not evidence, and neither are a dissenter's.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Kary_Mullis (1983 conception while driving, Cetus employment, first PCR experiments and Taq adoption, $10,000 bonus, 1987 patents 4,683,195 and 4,683,202, Cetus-to-Roche sale for $300M on 23 July 1991, 1993 Nobel shared with Michael Smith, documented HIV/AIDS and climate positions, death 2019); grokipedia.com/page/Polymerase_chain_reaction and grokipedia.com/page/Taq_polymerase (thermostable polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, 20-40 cycles, denature/anneal/extend); nobelprize.org Kary B. Mullis Nobel lecture (Highway 128 to Mendocino, mile marker 46.7, April 1983, first successful run December 1983) -- note this CORRECTS Grokipedia's 'Highway 17'
framing_note: vision_mandated TRUE because the closing rung is the sub-strand's guardrail on the bank's own dissent arc. The bank does NOT endorse Mullis's HIV/AIDS or climate claims, and equally must NOT sneer at dissent as such; the rung teaches exactly ONE thing -- a prize is for a result, not a warrant of universal correctness -- and it must state that the evidence HIV causes AIDS is overwhelming while still naming accurately what Mullis said. Present, never preach. Accuracy rails: it was Highway 128 toward Mendocino, mile marker 46.7, April 1983 (secondary sources including Grokipedia say Highway 17 -- that is WRONG; Mullis's own Nobel lecture and Scientific American account say 128); the first successful PCR run was December 1983 and the Saiki et al. Science paper came in 1985; Taq polymerase came from Brock and Freeze's 1969 Yellowstone isolate and NOT from Mullis. Dinner-test payoff: the Yellowstone hot-spring rung. Distractor mine: real adjacent techniques that do different jobs -- bacterial cloning, gel electrophoresis, restriction enzymes, Sanger sequencing -- plus real adjacent people (Saiki, Brock, Smith). Anti-restatement: never explain in the stem that the enzyme must survive boiling before asking where the enzyme came from.
history_overlap: history bank may cover the COVID pandemic as a recent-history episode and the science bank's own COVID-policy strand owns the cycle-threshold and test-policy disputes -- this ladder must stay on the invention, the enzyme, and contamination discipline.

name: DNA fingerprinting: the morning of 10 September 1984
scope: A genetic barcode, and the first thing it ever did in a murder case. T1: at about five past nine on the morning of Monday 10 September 1984, Alec Jeffreys lifted an X-ray film out of a developing tank in a Leicester darkroom and found a messy ladder of bands -- and within minutes understood that the mess was different for every person and visibly inherited from both parents. T2: what the bands are -- 'minisatellites', short stretches of DNA repeated over and over, where the NUMBER of repeats varies wildly between people because repeat counts mutate thousands of times faster than ordinary DNA. Jeffreys had been hunting variable markers for years for a completely different reason; the barcode was a by-product. T3: the first real use was not a crime at all -- in April 1985 the technique reunited a family. A Ghanaian boy refused entry to Britain was proved to be his mother's son by reconstructing his absent father's profile from his siblings, and an immigration tribunal decision was overturned. Jeffreys credits his wife with spotting that application. T3: the Enderby case -- in 1986 Leicestershire police brought Jeffreys two linked murders. A seventeen-year-old, Richard Buckland, had already CONFESSED to one of them. The DNA did not match him. The very first use of DNA evidence in a murder inquiry FREED an innocent man who had confessed -- and demonstrated, in a way no argument could, that a confession can be false. T4: with no suspect left, the police ran the world's first mass DNA screen -- blood and saliva from more than four thousand local men. It found nobody, because the killer had sent a substitute: Colin Pitchfork persuaded a colleague, Ian Kelly, to give a sample in his name. Kelly talked about it in a pub, a woman who overheard it eventually told the police, and Pitchfork was convicted on 22 January 1988 -- the first murder conviction obtained through DNA. T5: what a 'match' actually is -- a probability statement about how rare a pattern is in some reference population, not a photograph and not a fingerprint in the old sense; the honest number depends on the database used and on assumptions about relatives. T5: modern methods amplify from so few cells that DNA transferred by a handshake or a shared doorknob can put an innocent person at a scene they never visited -- sensitivity created a new way to be wrong. T5: the inventor's own warning -- Jeffreys has argued publicly against indefinitely retaining DNA profiles from people never convicted of anything, describing it as branding hundreds of thousands of innocent people as criminals. T5: the technology's largest single achievement is subtraction -- hundreds of wrongful convictions overturned, starting with Buckland.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys (approx. 9:05 a.m. on 10 September 1984 in Leicester, minisatellites with mutation rates up to 10,000x baseline, two Nature papers 10 January 1985, April 1985 Ghanaian immigration case reconstructing the absent father's profile from siblings, Leicestershire police approach August 1986, Buckland's exclusion in early 1987 as the first exoneration by DNA, mass screen of 4,000+ men, Pitchfork conviction 22 January 1988, Jeffreys' 2008-2009 objections to retaining profiles of the unconvicted, 200+ wrongful convictions resolved); grokipedia.com/page/Colin_Pitchfork (Ian Kelly substitution, the overheard pub conversation, screening of ~5,000 men born 1953-1970, guilty plea January 1988)
framing_note: The sub-strand's cleanest 'a test can defeat a confession' story. TONE RAIL, load-bearing for a kids' bank: the victims were two fifteen-year-old girls -- name the case, never dwell on the crimes, and put the ladder's emotional centre on Buckland walking free, not on the killer. Dinner-test payoff: the confession that DNA overturned. Accuracy rails: 9:05 a.m., Monday 10 September 1984, Leicester -- Jeffreys's own repeatedly documented account, so use it precisely; the ORDER matters and is the whole point of the ladder -- the technique's first application was the 1985 immigration case, its first murder-case use was an exoneration, and the conviction came third; a DNA 'match' is a probability, never a certainty, and the bank should teach that before testing it. Distractor mine: real adjacent forensics -- ABO blood typing, actual ridge fingerprints, hair microscopy and bite-mark comparison (the last two are genuine forensic methods since largely discredited, which is squarely on-voice). Anti-restatement: never say 'the crime-scene sample did not match Buckland' in a stem that asks what the first murder-case use of DNA accomplished.
history_overlap: history bank may own the fate of the Romanov family -- the 1993 DNA identification of the Romanov remains (work Jeffreys was involved in) is a real duplication risk; keep this ladder on Leicester, the immigration case and the method.

name: The Human Genome Project and the 20,000-gene surprise
scope: Reading three billion letters, and being wrong about what they would say. T2: the scale -- about three billion base pairs, formally begun on 1 October 1990 with a fifteen-year plan and a three-billion-dollar budget; it came in under both, about $2.7 billion, declared essentially complete on 14 April 2003, deliberately timed to the fiftieth anniversary of the double helix. T3: the race -- in May 1998 Craig Venter announced that Celera Genomics would do it privately in three years for roughly $300 million using whole-genome shotgun sequencing (smash the entire genome at random and let computers reassemble it) against the public consortium's slower map-first method. The public side under Francis Collins pulled its own deadline forward and bound itself to release every finished stretch into a public database within twenty-four hours -- the Bermuda Principles agreed in 1996. T3: the truce -- on 26 June 2000 Bill Clinton hosted both sides at the White House with Tony Blair on a satellite link to announce a joint 'working draft': a political draw whose real consequence was that the human sequence stayed free. T4: the surprise. Before the project, the working guess was 100,000 human genes or more -- one for roughly each protein we thought we needed. A betting pool run by Ewan Birney took more than 460 wagers from working scientists, some above 200,000; it was won in 2003 by Lee Rowen with 25,947. The draft said 26,000 to 40,000. The settled answer is about 20,000 protein-coding genes (19,969 in the finished 2022 sequence) -- roughly what a millimetre-long nematode worm has, and fewer than rice. Complexity is not gene count. T4: only about 1.5% of the human genome codes for protein at all. T5 (contested, and the bank says so): the other 98.5% was long written off as 'junk'. In September 2012 the ENCODE consortium reported that more than 80% of the genome shows biochemical activity, and headlines announced the death of junk DNA. Dan Graur and other evolutionary biologists attacked the claim hard, arguing that 'something binds it or transcribes it' is not the same as 'it does a job that natural selection maintains'; ENCODE later clarified it had meant biochemical function specifically. Large amounts of real regulatory DNA certainly exist; how much of the remainder matters is genuinely unsettled, and no rung may pretend otherwise. T5: the 'finished' 2003 genome was not finished -- roughly 8%, some 200 million bases of repetitive centromere and telomere sequence, could not be read with the technology of the day; the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium closed the last gaps on 31 March 2022 using ultra-long-read sequencing. T5: honest accounting -- sequencing a genome has fallen from billions of dollars to under a thousand, and the medicine promised from that White House podium has arrived unevenly: real cures for a short list of single-gene diseases, powerful risk statistics for common ones, and far fewer cures than the speeches implied.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project (launched 1 October 1990, Celera founded 9 May 1998 with a 3-year/$300M plan, Bermuda Principles February 1996, 26 June 2000 Clinton and Blair announcement, 14 April 2003 completion at ~$2.7 billion on the double helix's 50th anniversary, 92% coverage with <400 gaps, pre-project estimates exceeding 100,000 genes, drafts at 26,000-40,000, 2005 revision to 20,000-25,000, protein-coding exons ~1.5%, T2T CHM13 gapless assembly 31 March 2022 and 19,969 protein-coding genes, post-HGP therapeutic shortfall); grokipedia.com/page/ENCODE (September 2012 publications, the >80% biochemically active claim, Dan Graur's critique, ENCODE's later clarification, media overinterpretation); genome.gov GeneSweep exhibit and Science 300:1484 (Birney's pool, 460+ bets, Lee Rowen's winning 25,947 announced 30 May 2003)
framing_note: Two invertible hooks, both first-rate. Dinner-test payoff: the gene-count rung -- put 100,000 (and the betting pool, and the 200,000-gene wagers) in the STEM as what everyone confidently expected, and let the kid supply what actually turned up. Accuracy rails: always say 'protein-coding genes' when quoting ~20,000, because counting RNA genes gives a different and larger number and the sloppy version is the commonest error; the popular 'fewer genes than a grape' line is true for several plants but is a slippery cross-species comparison -- if the bank uses it, use a checkable example (rice has more annotated genes than a human) and say why the comparison is loose; the ENCODE 80% claim is CONTESTED and the bank must name who contested it (Graur and colleagues) and on what ground, and must never let a distractor smuggle in 'junk DNA is all functional' as settled fact. MYSTERY mode is explicitly licensed on the non-coding rung -- 'no one yet knows how much of it does real work' is the correct answer and should be said proudly. Distractor mine: pre-2000 gene estimates, the two genuinely rival sequencing strategies, and real named principals (Venter, Collins, Sulston, Birney, Graur). Anti-restatement: never let a stem mention 'only 1.5% codes for protein' before asking what the junk-DNA argument is about.

name: Epigenetics and the Dutch Hunger Winter
scope: Marks written on top of the code -- how far they reach, and how far they do not. T2: the version you can see from the pavement -- every calico or tortoiseshell cat is a patchwork produced by gene silencing. Early in a female mammal's development, each cell shuts down one of its two X chromosomes at random and keeps it shut in every daughter cell forever, so the coat is a map of which X won where. Mary Lyon proposed this in 1961 from variegated mouse coats, and it is why an ordinary calico cat is almost always female. T3: the chemistry -- a methyl group, one carbon and three hydrogens, parked on a cytosine can silence a gene without altering a single letter of the sequence, and the pattern is copied when the cell divides. The code stays identical; the annotations on it change. T3: a controlled demonstration -- Robert Waterland and Randy Jirtle (2003) fed pregnant agouti mice a diet rich in methyl donors (folic acid, vitamin B12, choline, betaine). Their pups were born brown and lean instead of yellow and obese: the same genes, differently methylated at a transposable element sitting beside the agouti gene. T4: the human case, and why it exists -- in the German-blockaded western Netherlands, rations fell below 1,000 calories a day from November 1944 and to roughly 500 by April 1945; about 4.5 million people were affected and some 20,000 died. Dutch record-keeping never stopped, so the babies carried through that famine became one of the best-documented natural experiments in human biology, with exact exposure dates. T4: the finding -- people conceived during the famine, and only those exposed right around conception, showed measurably lower methylation of the imprinted IGF2 gene than their own unexposed brothers and sisters, in blood sampled SIXTY YEARS later; that same group carried higher rates of obesity and metabolic disease in adulthood. A few months of hunger before birth left a chemical annotation for a lifetime. T5 (the honest limit, and the point of the ladder): does it reach the grandchildren? In plants and in nematode worms, inherited epigenetic marks are solidly demonstrated. In mammals the germ line wipes most methylation twice -- once in the primordial germ cells and again after fertilisation -- and the human evidence for true transgenerational transmission to grandchildren and beyond is thin, indirect and confounded. The bank's answer is: not established, and anyone who tells a child otherwise is ahead of the data. T5 (corrected misconception): epigenetics is constantly reported as 'Lamarck was right after all'. He was not. Nothing here shows a giraffe's stretched neck being inherited; what is shown is a regulatory setting altered by environment, on a genome whose sequence is unchanged, and which is usually reset between generations. T5: what the machinery is actually FOR -- it is not a curiosity, it is how one identical genome builds a neuron and a liver cell in the same body. The mark is the reason a cell remembers what it is.
source: grokipedia.com/page/Dutch_famine_of_1944-1945 (rations below 1,000 kcal from November 1944, below 600 by March and ~500 by April 1945, ~4.3-4.5 million affected, ~20,000-22,000 deaths, Operation Manna airdrops from 29 April 1945, prenatal exposure effects on birth weight and adult metabolic disease, IGF2 hypomethylation of about 5% versus unexposed siblings measured 60 years later); grokipedia.com/page/Epigenetics and grokipedia.com/page/Transgenerational_epigenetic_inheritance (methylation mechanism, two waves of germline and post-fertilisation reprogramming, TEI well established in plants and C. elegans but 'indirect and controversial' in humans, the Lamarck framing debate); grokipedia.com/page/X-inactivation (Mary Lyon 1961 from variegated mouse coat colour, random silencing, mosaicism, Barr body); Waterland & Jirtle, Mol Cell Biol 23:5293 (2003) via depts.washington.edu PDF (methyl-donor diet, agouti coat colour and metabolic phenotype)
framing_note: MECHANISM plus MYSTERY, with a corrected-misconception rung as the spine. The T5 restraint rung is the reason this ladder exists: it is the sub-strand's proof that the bank will say 'not established' about a fashionable idea even when the fashionable version is the better story. Accuracy rails, hard: the Heijmans 2008 result is periconceptional exposure only, at IGF2, roughly 5% lower methylation against same-sex SIBLING controls, sixty years on -- never inflate it to 'the famine rewrote their DNA'; the grandchild evidence in the Dutch cohort is weak, so no rung may claim 'the mark was passed to the grandchildren'; state every time that methylation does not change the DNA sequence. Dinner-test payoff: the calico cat -- a walking epigenetics demonstration on any street, and a genuine test-it-yourself invitation (find a calico, predict its sex, explain the patches). Distractor mine: Lamarckian use-inheritance, ordinary mutation, genetic drift, and plain undernutrition with no molecular mechanism -- all plausible-sounding and all wrong here. Anti-restatement: describe what was measured in the siblings' blood and let the mechanism be recalled, never define methylation in a stem that asks what silenced the gene.
history_overlap: history bank owns the Dutch Hunger Winter as a WWII episode (the September 1944 railway strike, the German food embargo, Operation Manna) -- this ladder may set the scene in one clause but must key the SCIENTIFIC opportunity (an accidental controlled experiment with intact birth records) and the IGF2 finding; the animal bank owns cat breeds and coat adaptation, so the calico rung must key X-inactivation as a cell-biology mechanism, not the cat.
